title: Class → object → self
blurb: A class is the blueprint; each call builds a new object, and self is the object the method was called on.

steps.note: The class statement runs its body from top to bottom. Nothing is an object yet: this builds the blueprint.
def creates the function __init__ and stores it in the class body namespace. It does not run yet.
volume is created the same way. Both functions end up inside the class (blueprint #1).
Cuboid(10, 5, 3) creates a brand-new EMPTY object (#2) and calls __init__ with that object as self. Python passes self for you.
self.length = l creates the attribute length INSIDE the object that self points to.
breadth is added to the same object.
height is added. __init__ is finished, so the object now has 3 attributes.
A second call builds a second, separate object (#3). The same __init__ runs again, but self now points to #3.
self.length = l creates the attribute length INSIDE the object that self points to.
breadth is added to the same object.
height is added. __init__ is finished, so the object now has 3 attributes.
c1.volume() is the same as Cuboid.volume(c1): self points to #2, the object of c1.
The method reads length, breadth and height through self (#2) and returns 10 x 5 x 3 = 150. print then shows it.
c2.volume(): same code, but self points to #3, so the answer is different.
Same method, self is #3: 2 x 3 x 4 = 24. One method, many objects: self decides which one.

title: Instance variables: where they are born
blurb: a is created by __init__, b only when func() runs, c is added from outside. All three live in the object, not in the class.

steps.note: The class statement runs its body and builds the blueprint.
Test() creates an empty object and calls __init__.
self.a = 10 creates instance variable a. __init__ runs on every object creation, so a always exists.
t3.func() runs func with self = t3.
self.b = 20 creates b, but only because func() was called. Instance variables created in other methods exist only after that method runs.
t3.c = 30 adds c from OUTSIDE the class, through the object name. It works, but only this object has c.
t3.show() reads a, b and c. All three exist now, so no error.
self.a exists, so a = 10 is printed.
self.b exists (func() ran), so b = 20 is printed.
self.c exists (added from outside), so c = 30 is printed.

title: Instance variable that does not exist yet
blurb: show() reads self.b, but func() never ran, so b was never created. (Intentional error from instanceVariable.py)

steps.note: The class statement runs its body and builds the blueprint.
t1 = Test() calls __init__ only. func() is never called.
t1.show() starts. self points to t1, which has only a.
a exists, so a = 10 is printed.
self.b is read, but b was never created because func() did not run. Python raises AttributeError. Line 9 (c) is never reached.

title: A validator that can be bypassed
blurb: set_length() guards the value, but r.length = -10 walks around it because the variable is public.

steps.note: The class statement builds the blueprint.
Rectangle(5, 10) creates an empty object and calls __init__.
__init__ does not assign length directly. It calls the validator set_length through self.
The validator checks the rule: length must be greater than 0.
5 > 0, so length = 5 is stored in the object.
breadth is stored. Construction is finished.
r.length = -10 writes straight to the variable. The validator is NOT called, so the bad value is stored. This is why we need @property or private names.
The accessor now returns -10: the rule was bypassed.

title: Class (static) variable and @classmethod
blurb: count lives once in the class object. Every new Rectangle bumps the same counter.

steps.note: The class statement runs its body. Variables written directly in the body become CLASS variables.
count = 0 is created once, in the class object (#1), not in any instance.
A plain method whose first parameter happens to be named cls. It is still an INSTANCE method.
length is an instance variable: stored in the object.
breadth is an instance variable too.
Rectangle.count += 1 changes the one shared copy in the class: 0 becomes 1.
length is an instance variable: stored in the object.
breadth is an instance variable too.
The second object bumps the SAME counter: 1 becomes 2. Both objects see 2.
r1.func_area() uses instance variables of r1.
Calling a classmethod through the class passes the class as cls.
cls.count reads the shared class variable: 2.

title: Instance method called through the class
blurb: Rectangle.func_instance_getCount() has no object to bind to, so the first parameter is missing. (Intentional error from classVariable.py)

steps.note: The class statement runs its body.
count = 0 is created once, in the class object.
func_instance_getCount is a normal method (its first parameter is only NAMED cls).
length is stored in the object.
breadth is stored in the object.
Through an object, the method gets the object as its first parameter (named cls here).
The first parameter is the object, so cls.count finds count through the object: 1.
Rectangle.func_instance_getCount() goes through the CLASS. A normal method called through the class gets no object, so the first parameter is missing: TypeError.
steps.error: TypeError: Rectangle.func_instance_getCount() missing 1 required positional argument: 'cls'

title: Static method: no self, no cls
blurb: A @staticmethod is just a function that lives in the class. It works through the class or through an object.

steps.note: The class statement runs its body.
func_area is a plain function stored in the class. Its first parameter is just called length.
@staticmethod marks the function below as "do not pass self".
Calling a plain function through the CLASS: nothing is passed automatically, so (5, 10) bind to length and breadth.
A static method called through an OBJECT still receives no self. (5, 10) bind to length and breadth.
Through the class: same result. A static method works both ways.

title: Plain function called through an object
blurb: r.func_area(5, 10) passes r as the first argument automatically, so 3 arguments reach a 2-parameter function. (Intentional error from staticMethod.py)

steps.note: The class statement runs its body.
r.func_area(5, 10): through an object, Python inserts r as the first argument automatically. That makes 3 arguments (r, 5, 10) for a function with 2 parameters, so Python raises TypeError.
steps.error: TypeError: Rectangle.func_area() takes 2 positional arguments but 3 were given

title: @property getter and setter
blurb: r.length looks like a plain attribute but calls the getter; r.length = -9 calls the setter, which clamps it to 1.

steps.note: The class statement runs its body from top to bottom.
@property is evaluated and then applied to the getter below.
@length.setter looks up the name length in the class body. It exists only because the getter above already created it. Setter before getter would be a NameError.
The value is kept in the "private" _length, not in length.
r.length reads through the property: Python calls the getter.
r.length = -9 calls the setter instead of writing a variable.
The setter validates: is the new length greater than 0?
-9 is not valid, so the setter stores 1 instead.
Reading r.length again calls the getter.
The getter returns the clamped value, 1.

title: Private names and name mangling
blurb: __private_variable is stored as _Parent__private_variable. Writing child.__private_variable from outside creates a different attribute.

steps.note: class Child(Parent) builds Child; Parent is its base class.
Child(5, 10, 15) creates object #3 and calls Child.__init__.
super().__init__ runs Parent.__init__ on the same object.
public_variable is stored under its own name.
A single underscore is only a convention: _protected_variable is stored as is.
Inside class Parent, self.__private_variable is rewritten to _Parent__private_variable. This is name mangling.
func_show_variables is defined in Parent, so it uses the mangled name that Parent created. It finds all three.
Outside any class there is no mangling. This creates a NEW attribute literally named __private_variable. The real private one is untouched.
Same method again: it still prints 5 for the private one.
Writing the mangled name _Parent__private_variable replaces the "private" value. Private in Python is a naming trick, not a lock.

title: Child cannot see the parent's private name
blurb: Inside Child, self.__private_variable is mangled to _Child__private_variable, which does not exist. (Intentional error from dataHiding.py)

steps.note: Child(5, 10, 15) creates object #3 and calls Child.__init__.
super().__init__ runs Parent.__init__ on the same object.
Parent.__init__ stores the private value as _Parent__private_variable.
Public variables are visible to child classes.
Protected (single underscore) is visible to child classes too.
Inside class Child, self.__private_variable is rewritten to self._Child__private_variable. The object has _Parent__private_variable, not that, so AttributeError.

title: Inheritance and super().__init__
blurb: Cuboid has its own __init__, so Rectangle.__init__ only runs because Cuboid calls super().__init__.

steps.note: class Cuboid(Rectangle): Cuboid inherits everything from Rectangle.
def creates Cuboid.__init__. It will replace the inherited one.
Cuboid(5, 10, 20) creates object #3 and calls Cuboid.__init__ (the child one wins).
height is stored first. The object has only height so far: length and breadth do not exist yet.
super().__init__(l, b) calls the PARENT constructor on the same object. Without this line Rectangle.__init__ would never run.
Now the parent constructor stores length.
and breadth. The stack shows two __init__ frames on top of each other.
Uses height, length and breadth: 20 x 5 x 10 = 1000.

title: Method Resolution Order (mixed inheritance)
blurb: Python searches Child4, then Parent5 and its parent, then Parent6 and its parent, then object.

steps.note: Child4 inherits from Parent5 first, then Parent6.
mro() lists the lookup order: Child4, Parent5, Grandparent2, Parent6, GrandParent3, object. Each parent chain is finished before the next base class starts (depth first, left to right).

title: Method overriding
blurb: Child defines show() too, so Child().show() runs the child version. The parent version is shadowed.

steps.note: def creates Child.show: same name as the parent method.
Child() creates object #3 and calls Child.__init__.
super().__init__() runs Parent.__init__ to create the parent variable.
child.show(): Python looks in Child first and finds show there. Parent.show is shadowed and never runs.
Prints the child variable. Parent.show would only run if Child.show called super().show().

title: Abstract class: child implements the abstract method
blurb: Child overrides meth2, so it is concrete and can be instantiated. meth1 is inherited from Parent.

steps.note: Imports ABC (abstract base class helper) and the abstractmethod decorator.
class Parent(ABC): any class that inherits ABC can be abstract.
def creates meth1, a concrete method with a body (shared code).
@abstractmethod marks meth2 as a method children MUST override. Parent now has an unimplemented abstract method, so Parent is abstract.
def creates Child.meth2: this overrides the abstract method, so Child is no longer abstract.
Child() works because every abstract method is overridden.
Calls the child version of meth2.
meth1 is inherited from Parent (shared code).

title: Abstract class cannot be instantiated (extra)
blurb: Extra example for the PDF rule "abstract means cannot be instantiated". Parent() is refused before any object exists.

steps.note: @abstractmethod marks meth2 as mandatory for children, which makes Parent abstract.
Parent() is refused: a class with an unimplemented abstract method cannot be instantiated. No object is created.
steps.error: TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class Parent without an implementation for abstract method 'meth2'

title: Operator overloading: v1 + v2
blurb: The + sign calls vector1.__add__(vector2), which builds and returns a new Vector.

steps.note: def creates __add__, the method behind the + sign.
vector1 + vector2 is turned into vector1.__add__(vector2): self is #2, other is #3.
isinstance checks that other really is a Vector.
A new Vector(4, 6) is built (object #4) and returned. The two originals are untouched.

title: Polymorphism and duck typing
blurb: person() never checks the type. Anything with talk() and walk() works.

steps.note: person is an ordinary function. Its parameter pet has no type.
person(dog): pet is bound to the Dog object.
pet.talk() runs whatever talk the object has.
The same person() now receives a Duck. Same name, different action: polymorphism.
pet.talk() runs whatever talk the object has.

title: Inner (nested) class
blurb: Outer builds an Inner object in __init__ and keeps it in self.in_obj. Outer reaches Inner through that attribute.

steps.note: class Inner is written inside Outer, so it becomes a member of Outer, like a method.
Outer() creates object and calls Outer.__init__.
self.Inner() finds the Inner class through the object, builds an Inner object and stores it as in_obj.
The Inner object stores its own data.
Outer hands the work to its Inner object.
Reaching through outer.in_obj gives direct access to the Inner object and its method.

title: Calling an inner method on the outer object
blurb: func_show belongs to Inner, not Outer. (Intentional error from InnerClass.py)

steps.note: class Inner is written inside Outer.
Outer() creates the outer object, which builds and keeps an Inner object.
The Inner object stores its data.
outer.func_show() asks the OUTER object for a method that only Inner has, so Python raises AttributeError.

title: Nested Task class + heapq priority queue
blurb: heappush keeps the smallest (priority, task) tuple at index 0, so peek and pop always see the most urgent task.

steps.note: The class statement for PriorityScheduler starts.
class Task is nested inside PriorityScheduler.
task_list starts as an empty list.
self.Task(...) builds a Task object through the outer object.
priority stored in the Task (the attribute is spelled "prioirty" in the source).
heappush stores the tuple (2, task). One item, so it is trivially the smallest.
self.Task(...) builds a Task object through the outer object.
priority stored in the Task (the attribute is spelled "prioirty" in the source).
heappush adds (1, task) and moves it to the front: index 0 always holds the smallest tuple.
peek_task() only looks at the smallest.
nsmallest(1, ...) returns a new list with the smallest tuple. The heap is unchanged.
next_task() removes and returns the smallest.
peek again: only priority 2 is left.
nsmallest(1, ...) returns a new list with the smallest tuple. The heap is unchanged.

title: SortedList with bisect
blurb: insort keeps the list sorted on every insert; bisect_left answers where a value would go. (Driver lines at the bottom are added for the Lab.)

steps.note: Imports bisect under the short name bi.
values starts as an empty list.
insort puts 30 into the sorted list: [30].
insort finds the right place for 10 (before 30): [10, 30].
insort puts 20 between them: [10, 20, 30]. The list stays sorted without sorting again.
bisect_left finds index 2 (after 20, before 30) without changing the list.
